newsitem.title: UK: Cut off from trade with U.S., Iran woos Britain.
newsitem.headline: Cut off from trade with U.S., Iran woos Britain.

text.p: Cut off by U.S. sanctions from the world's single largest market, Iran on Tuesday promoted itself as a reliable trade partner to industrialists in Britain, the only major OECD country to increase exports to Tehran in 1995.

Several senior Iranian officials told a conference sponsored by the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) that business is booming and the economy thriving in Iran despite Washington's attempts to punish non-U.S. firms from investing there.
They said Iran's mineral riches and cultural and political ties to central Asia not to mention its youthful 61 million strong population makes it too important a market to ignore.

"Due to communications and interdependency amongst nations, as well as the undeniable potential and abilities of Iran, it would be almost impossible and indeed impractical to isolate her," Gholamreza Ansari, Iran's London Charge d'affaires, said.

He and other Iranian officials at the conference said Washington's trade and investment ban and a later law designed to punish foreign companies investing more than $40 million in Iran seems to have won Tehran more friends.
Deputy Oil Minister Mohammed Hedi Nejad Hosseinian said European Union protests against the U.S. legislation had helped smooth negotiations with foreign oil companies.
"The political environment for doing these projects is now better than before," he said.

Britain shows no signs of shying away from business with Tehran. Ray Mingay, director general of export promotion at the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) said London "welcomed an overall increase in bilateral trade" with Iran.
"The potential trading partnership is much more significant than at present," Mingay said.
In 1995, Britain's visible exports to Iran amounted to 332 million pounds ($556 million), 15 percent up on 1994. In the first six months of 1996, the figure hit 180 million.
As the world's third largest oil exporter and second only to Russia in natural gas reserves, Iran's greatest asset is its hydrocarbons industry.

Hosseinian said Iran hoped to award its first oil and gas investment projects to foreign companies within the next three months. He said there were plenty of foreign companies from Europe and other regions interested in the 10 "buy-back" projects open to tender.
But a campaign to lessen its dependency on oil also is paying off, officials said.

At the end of the current fiscal year ending in March 1997, total exports are expected to pass $20 billion with non-oil exports expected to reach $5 billion, said Mohammad Nahavandian, deputy commerce minister.

He said during the government's first "Five Year Plan" which ended in 1994, non-oil exports made an "ambitious leap" from $800 million to $4.3 billion and should pass the target of $6.16 billion in the second "Five Year Plan" before it ends in 2000.

The rest of Iran's economy is booming, officials said. Inflation is set to fall to below 20 percent next year from nearly 50 percent in 1995 and 23.1 percent in October 1996, said Central Bank Vice Governor Ahmad Azizi.

Azizi said gross domestic product (GDP) is expected to grow 4.5 percent this year versus 1.6 percent last year while in the financial year ended March 1996, some $5.7 billion of short and medium term debt was repaid and 80 percent of the outstanding debt switched to long and medium term. -- London newsroom, +44 171 542 6280 ($1=.5970 Pound)
